Lithium is a noun that refers to a chemical element — one of the fundamental building blocks of matter found in nature. It is a metal, but unlike the metals most people picture (iron, gold, copper), lithium is strikingly unusual. It is the lightest metal in existence and, in fact, one of the lightest solid substances on Earth. It is so light that it can float on water. It is soft enough that you could slice through it with a knife, and it has a silvery-white appearance when freshly cut.

On the periodic table — the organized chart of all chemical elements — lithium holds position number 3, and its chemical symbol is Li.

Lithium is extremely reactive. This means it doesn't just sit quietly; it actively "wants" to combine with other substances. If you expose it to air, it reacts with oxygen and moisture almost immediately, which is why it must be stored carefully (typically under oil or in sealed containers). If you place a piece of lithium in water, it reacts vigorously, fizzing and releasing hydrogen gas.

This high reactivity is actually the key to why lithium is so valuable — it stores and releases energy very efficiently.

Lithium doesn't exist freely in nature in its pure metal form (because it's too reactive and immediately bonds with other elements). Instead, it is found locked inside rocks and minerals, and dissolved in the water of certain salt flats and brine lakes. The largest deposits of lithium in the world are found in South America — particularly in the salt flats of Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina — as well as in Australia and certain parts of China.

To get usable lithium, companies mine these sources and process them chemically to extract the element.
The Two Most Important Uses of Lithium

1. Lithium-ion batteries

This is the most common reason you hear the word "lithium" in everyday life today. Lithium is the core ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, the type of rechargeable battery that powers almost every modern electronic device — your smartphone, laptop, tablet, electric car, and more.

Why is lithium used in batteries? Because it is the lightest metal and has an exceptionally strong ability to store and release electrical energy. A lithium battery can hold a large amount of energy in a small, lightweight package. When you charge your phone, you are forcing lithium ions to move and store energy; when your phone runs, those ions move back and release that energy. This movement of ions is the fundamental mechanism behind all lithium-ion batteries.

This has made lithium one of the most strategically important materials of the 21st century. As the world shifts toward electric vehicles and renewable energy (which requires large batteries to store power from solar panels and wind turbines), the demand for lithium has skyrocketed. It is sometimes called "white gold" because of how economically valuable it has become.

2. Lithium in medicine (psychiatry)

Lithium also has a significant role in medicine, specifically in psychiatry. Lithium compounds — most commonly lithium carbonate (a salt of lithium) — are used as a mood-stabilizing medication. When doctors or patients say someone is "on lithium," this is what they mean.

It is primarily prescribed to people with bipolar disorder, a condition characterized by extreme swings between manic episodes (periods of abnormally high energy, impulsiveness, and elevated mood) and depressive episodes (periods of deep sadness and low energy). Lithium helps smooth out these extreme swings, keeping a person's mood more stable.

How it works in the brain is not completely understood even by scientists, but lithium affects certain chemical signaling pathways in the brain that regulate mood. It is one of the oldest psychiatric medications still in use today and, for many patients, remains one of the most effective.

Lithium as a medication requires careful monitoring through blood tests, because the therapeutic range — the amount that is helpful versus harmful — is narrow. Too little and it doesn't work; too much can be toxic.

Beyond batteries and medicine, lithium has some other uses worth knowing:

  • Ceramics and glass: Lithium compounds are used to make certain special glasses and ceramics stronger and more heat-resistant (like the glass on some cooktops and telescopes).
  • Lubricants: Lithium-based greases are used in machinery to reduce friction at both very high and very low temperatures — in airplane parts, for example.
  • Nuclear applications: Lithium plays a role in nuclear technology; one of its isotopes (a variant of the element) is used in hydrogen bomb designs and is being researched for nuclear fusion energy.

Lithium as a noun means a specific chemical element — the lightest metal, highly reactive, silvery in color, found in minerals and salt flats. In practical everyday use, the word almost always refers to one of two things: lithium-ion batteries (the power source of modern technology) or lithium-based psychiatric medication (a treatment for bipolar disorder). Both uses exist because of the same fundamental chemical properties that make lithium reactive, lightweight, and excellent at interacting with charged particles and biological systems.
